//: Copy this to ~/.config/claude-code-toolkit/config.json and edit. `install.sh` does
that for you if the file does not exist yet. Nothing here is committed —
the config lives outside the repo so it cannot leak and survives a re-clone.
Every key is optional. Omit one and the tool falls back to a documented
default; omit the whole file and everything still runs, with the danger
guard in its STRICTEST mode (see workspace_root below).
Paths may use ~, $VAR and ${VAR}. In the guards' keys, a path naming an unset
variable is ignored (treated as absent), so it can never widen what is trusted.
//owner_name: Your first name, e.g. "owner_name": "Sam". Named when the guard tells Claude to hand a command back to you. Absent means 'the human'; /onboard and ./install.sh --setup fill it in. Deliberately not set here: install.sh copies this file verbatim on a no-TTY install, and a placeholder would become a live name.
//profiles: Which toolkit profiles (plugins) this machine installs, e.g. ["continuity", "builder"].
The five: core, continuity, builder, maintainer, mac. Not set in the live
keys: absent is the normal state. `core` is always implied. Default when
absent: the registry's default profiles, core + continuity (see
claude/profiles.json). Selecting maintainer brings builder, because the
registry's `requires` pulls it in. A present list replaces the default set
(core and anything a listed profile requires stay implied), so leaving out
continuity means install.sh does not install it, and install.sh warns.
Dropping a profile the last install selected uninstalls its plugin on the
next install (--check says it would), unless another installed plugin
depends on it; a toolkit plugin you enabled yourself is never touched. A
broken config file, null, a value that
is not a list, or an unknown name makes install.sh and --check exit 1.
lib/setup_config.py --profiles <list> writes this key (core added, requires
closure applied); choosing mac also sets caffeinate.enabled: true unless the

//workspace_root: The single tree your work lives in, e.g. "~/Work". Left null here so a
copy of this file keeps the strict default; setup writes the one you
choose, after checking it. The danger guard treats deletions
inside it as ordinary and deletions outside it as suspect.
NO DEFAULT, on purpose: unconfigured means the guard trusts nothing but
~/.claude, ~/bin and the temp dirs, so it errs strict rather than guessing
a root and silently widening what may be deleted.

//max_bytes: Tool-rules pages live in <workspace_root>/.claude/tool-rules/. There is no
directory key: the hook is inert without workspace_root.
Default 9500; absent (or not a positive integer) means 9500. The harness
drops hook output somewhere above ~10KB (a 9,871-char injection arrived
whole and a 10.9KB one did not). An over-cap page emits an overage line,

//unify: ON by default (absent = on; only literal false turns it off).
pointing EVERY session (repos, worktrees) at workspace_root's memory
folder. Skipped with a warning until a session has run in workspace_root.
false removes it again, but only if it still holds the toolkit's value.

//import: ON by default (absent = on; only literal false turns it off).
/onboard adds one line to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md that imports this
checkout's policy/CLAUDE.md, so the toolkit policy loads in every

verify warn when it is missing or dangling. false = the toolkit stops

nothing and --status reports opted-out. It does NOT remove an

//baseline_opt_out: Absent or empty = every rule in claude/permissions.baseline.json applies.
List exact `ask` rule strings from that file (e.g. "Bash(git push *)") to
stop install.sh re-adding them. `deny` rules cannot be opted out.
Nothing is removed from settings.json: delete the rule there by hand too.
This is personal policy; the shipped baseline stays as it is.

danger_guard.//extra_safe_roots: Additional trees where `rm` is routine. Never add a cloud-synced folder (Google Drive, Dropbox, iCloud) — a local delete there propagates everywhere.
danger_guard.//extra_protected_paths: Exact directories that must never be the rm target themselves, even though work happens inside them. Your repo roots belong here. `/`, $HOME, the workspace root, ~/.claude, ~/bin, ~/Documents, ~/Desktop and ~/Downloads are always protected and need no entry. Must be a list of paths that resolve: anything else (a single string, an unset $VAR) makes the guard refuse deletions until it is fixed, rather than silently dropping the protection.

//max_concurrent: How many claude-local-ci check runs may execute at once on this
machine, across every repo. A run that finds every slot taken prints
that it is waiting and blocks in the foreground until one frees up.
Slots are flock()ed files under ~/.cache/claude-local-ci/slots/, and
the kernel releases one the moment its holder exits, so a killed run
never strands a slot. Default 2 when absent or not a positive integer:
a third concurrent run on a small machine adds little throughput and
can produce a false red. Raise it on a bigger machine.

//canonical_root: The parent directory holding your canonical, one-folder-per-project
checkouts -- the ones ordinary edits should never land in directly,
because a parallel Claude Code session (or you, later) may be relying
on them staying put on their default branch.
This key switches on Rule C ONLY: blocking Edit/Write/MultiEdit/
NotebookEdit, commit, rebase, non-fast-forward merge, history-rewriting
push and remote-branch delete on the default branch of a checkout
directly under this root. Rule A (cross-checkout reach) and Rule B
(branch switching under concurrency) do not read it and still apply
everywhere regardless.
UNSET IS INACTIVE, NOT LENIENT, AND THERE IS NO FALLBACK. Rule C is
off unless THIS key names an existing directory. It is deliberately
NOT derived from workspace_root: turning a refusal ON is a decision
its owner makes, and deriving it would start blocking edits and
commits on the default branch of every checkout under a workspace
root set purely for the danger guard's benefit. A guessed root is
also worse than none for a guard: one naming a directory that is not
there is inactive and silent, which looks exactly like a guard with
nothing to say.
An older personal copy of this toolkit DID infer it, from
<workspace_root>/repos (or the workspace root when that was absent),
so a config carried over from it had Rule C on without this key. Run
`lib/setup_config.py <config> <repo> --report`: it shows the root
that copy would have used and the two commands, keep it
(--update --set worktree_guard.canonical_root=<root>) or leave Rule C
off (--update --set worktree_guard.canonical_root=null). Nothing is
written until you run one. Setup writes an explicit null, which is
how the report tells a decided config from an inherited one.
So: set this key explicitly, or Rule C does nothing. Rules A and B are
unaffected and need no configuration at all.

thread_handover.//enabled: Set false to turn off both the SessionStart pending-handover announcement and the UserPromptSubmit context watcher (claude-thread-deliver and claude-thread-watch). Defaults to true; absent means on. The /handover slash command itself is unaffected — this only silences the two background hooks that announce and nudge.
thread_handover.//handover_dir: Where /handover writes documents, and where the sweep retires them into archive/handovers/. Give it its own directory — the sweep moves files here. Setup writes <workspace_root>/handovers. null falls back to ~/.claude/handovers, where Claude Code asks before every write and a non-interactive session cannot write at all.
thread_handover.//caps: Context in tokens at which the watcher starts suggesting a handover, and at which it stops waiting for a natural boundary. Both are applied as min(cap, window x fraction), so a 200k-window model arms at 70k regardless. Lower arm_cap if a session usually ends before a natural boundary arrives.
//sweep_grace: How long an ATTACHED handover stays in the handover directory before the
sweep ARCHIVES it into archive/handovers/ — it is moved, never deleted. Both
gates must clear: that many distinct other sessions must have started AND
that many days must have passed since it was attached. Defaults to 3 and 7;
absent means those defaults, and a non-numeric value falls back to them too.
With several sessions open in one tree the session count is spent within
minutes (SessionStart fires per window and per /clear), so in practice
sweep_grace_days IS the grace period. It is exact wall clock: 3 means 72
hours from the attachment; at 7 a Friday-afternoon handover stays until the
following Friday, at 3 it is eligible on Monday. Lower it if handovers
linger too long for you, raise it if you want them to stay put longer.
Archiving moves the file into archive/handovers/ and keeps its name, so a
premature sweep costs a look in one more directory, not the document.
Do not set either key to 0 expecting to turn the sweep off; use
enabled: false for that. sweep_grace_days: 0 drops the day gate, so the
sweep archives as soon as the session count clears. sweep_grace_sessions: 0
is unpredictable rather than lenient: a record that was already seen by
another session is archived at the day floor, while one that never was is
kept forever.
A handover nobody ever attaches is never swept at all, and neither is one
whose index record cannot be dated. Clutter is the deliberate trade.

spec_archive.//enabled: Set false to make claude-spec-archive a no-op. Defaults to true; absent means on. This now also gates the SessionStart hook (--hook): false means the hook exits 0 silently and does nothing, same as an unset specs_dir.
//specs_dir: The directory of planning specs to manage, e.g. "~/Work/specs" (null
here, so a copy of this file moves nothing). THERE IS NO COMPILED DEFAULT:
absent means the tool prints 'not configured' and exits 0 having done
nothing. A tool that moves files must not guess which directory to move
them in, so the absent case is the inert one.
This is normally the same directory as thread_handover.handover_dir, and
the two tools coexist there deliberately. They never touch the same file:
spec-archive refuses anything matching the handover filename pattern, even
when it carries an archivable status, because that file belongs to the
handover sweep's own lifecycle — grace gates, an index row, a consuming
session. Two owners of one file is how a document gets lost. Both tools
now archive rather than delete (the sweep stopped deleting 2026-08-26),
and they still must not overlap: the sweep files into archive/handovers/,
which spec-archive skips along with the rest of archive/.
//min_age_days: How old a spec must be before a declared shipped/superseded status makes
it archivable. Defaults to 14; a non-numeric value falls back to that.
Compared strictly (age > min_age_days), so a file exactly at the boundary
is kept — the strict side is the default.
Unlike the handover sweep's grace gates, this floor is a convenience, not
a safety mechanism. The tool moves files into <specs_dir>/archive/ and
never deletes, so a wrong call costs a `mv` back. Lower it freely.
What actually protects a spec is its own front matter. A .md spec declares
`status: live | shipped | superseded` and `subject:` (the archive folder
slug); `live` is never archived at any age, and anything undeclared,
unparseable, or missing a subject is REPORTED and left alone rather than
filed under a guess. Paths that cannot carry front matter — directories,
basename. Front matter is read only for .md and the manifest only for
non-.md: they are non-overlapping by design, neither a fallback for the
other, so a break in one can never quietly cover for a break in the other.
//stale_flip_days: How many days a status: live spec must sit with its mtime unchanged, and
its 'Waiting on a human' section not open, before claude-spec-archive
--hook or --flip-stale flips it to status: shipped. Compared strictly
(age > stale_flip_days), same as min_age_days above. Unticked task boxes
(- [ ]) and open Backlog table rows also block the flip.
Defaults to 0; absent also means 0, and 0 means the flip is OFF — the
strict side is the default here, unlike min_age_days. Auto-archive (this
tool moving a spec someone already declared shipped/superseded) runs for
everyone regardless of this key; the flip is the one piece that is off
in the shipped default, because it rewrites the status line of a live
spec you never asked to have rewritten, where auto-archive only
ever moves a file someone already marked done. 21 is a reasonable
The write is narrow and recoverable: it changes only the front-matter
status: line (appending an auto-flipped marker), leaves every other byte
untouched, and resets the file's mtime on purpose — a freshly-flipped
spec then sits the ordinary min_age_days floor before archive will move
it. Set status: live back in the file to undo a wrong flip; it then
waits another stale_flip_days days before flipping again.
//hook_deadline_seconds: How many seconds the SessionStart hook (--hook) waits for its flip-and-
archive pass to finish before giving up and exiting 0 anyway. Defaults
to 4; a non-numeric or non-positive value falls back to 4 too.
This is a budget inside the hook's own declared timeout of 10 seconds in
plugin-build/hooks/hooks.json: the work runs on a daemon worker thread and
the main thread joins it with this deadline, so a stalled syscall is
bounded even though the worker thread itself cannot be killed. On
timeout the hook prints a 'did not finish' notice naming what already
completed and exits immediately, rather than letting Claude Code's own
kill at the declared timeout fire with no explanation.

repo_freshness.//enabled: Set false to silence the session-start notice that this repo is behind origin, and to stop the background fetch entirely. Defaults to true; absent means on.
repo_freshness.//fetch_interval_seconds: How stale the last `git fetch` may be before a new one is spawned in the background. Defaults to 14400 (4 hours). The fetch NEVER blocks the prompt — the notice is rendered from refs already on disk, so the only cost of a longer interval is finding out about an update one session later.
//watch: Repos to check besides claude-code-toolkit itself, which is always checked
(it is the repo the hook lives in, so it is found rather than configured).
Entries may be a bare repo name, resolved under <workspace_root>/repos/, or
a full path. An entry that is not a git checkout is skipped
silently, so listing a repo you have not cloned costs nothing.
Empty (the default) means the toolkit only.
Adding a repo is cheap because a repo is only ever reported when its HEAD is
ON its default branch. On a feature branch, being behind origin/main is not
staleness — it is what having a branch open means — so the notice stays quiet
until you switch back. That is what keeps a repo you actively develop in from
producing a daily warning nobody can act on.
One exception: a toolkit checkout pinned by ./install.sh --rollback is always
named, with the command that returns it.

sync.//enabled: Set true to let this hook run `git pull --ff-only` against every eligible repo under repo_root at session start (throttled by throttle_hours below). Defaults to false, and ONLY a literal JSON `true` turns it on -- the string "true", the number 1, or any other truthy-but-not-boolean value all still read as OFF, so a value that merely LOOKS like an opt-in can never become one by accident. A hook that rewrites working trees unattended must never arrive by upgrade.
sync.//repo_root: Where to look for repos to sync -- immediate subdirectories containing a .git are candidates; never recursed into. NO default, and nothing is derived from workspace_root: null, absent, or a path that is not an existing directory all mean the sync phase finds nothing to do. A tool that pulls working trees unattended never guesses which directory to pull in.
sync.//gh_owner: The GitHub account or org to discover NEW repos from (`gh repo list <gh_owner>`), cloning any not already present under repo_root. Has NO default -- absent means clone discovery is skipped entirely, with zero `gh` calls made. This is deliberate, not merely lenient: an owner is never inferred from an existing remote, git config, or `gh auth status`, because a personal `gh` login can often also see an organization it belongs to, and a guessed owner would risk sweeping a whole organization into someone's workspace unannounced.
sync.//throttle_hours: How often the sync phase (pull plus clone discovery) may run again, in hours. Defaults to 20; a non-integer value or one <= 0 also falls back to 20, so a bad value can never mean "every session".

tooling_digest.//enabled: Set false to stop injecting the tooling digest at session start. Defaults to true; absent means on. While it is on and no map file exists, every session starts with a one-line notice saying so and naming the command that turns it off: false is the quiet opt-out, a missing file is not.
//path: Your personal tooling/access map — what we use, how Claude reaches it,
and whether it currently works. null (the default) resolves to
<workspace_root>/TOOLING.md, which is what makes this portable: set
a workspace root and the feature works without naming a path.
The file is DELIBERATELY outside this repo. It describes one machine and
one set of accounts — which CLIs are installed, which account `gh` is
logged in as, which MCP connectors are authorized — so it is personal
config, not shared behaviour. Anything documented elsewhere stays
canonical there, and the map links to it rather than copying it.
Start from TOOLING.md.template in this repo. Only the marker-delimited
block is injected; everything else is read on demand. If neither this
key nor workspace_root is set, or the file does not exist or cannot be
read, the hook prints a one-line notice instead of a digest. Set
enabled to false to opt out quietly.
EITHER MARKER PAIR IS ACCEPTED: <!-- DIGEST:START --> / <!-- DIGEST:END -->
or <!-- CORE:START --> / <!-- CORE:END -->. They behave identically.
DIGEST predates the name and is what the template still ships; CORE is
the name the context contract uses. Accepting both is what makes the
contract landable without a migration.
The EARLIEST complete pair in the file wins, whichever kind it is — and
an empty pair is skipped in favour of the next populated one. Position
rather than marker kind, because a marker NAMED IN THE BODY (a code
fence documenting this very contract, for instance) must not be able to
outrank the file's real block. Precedence by kind was tried and let
exactly that happen. Carry ONE pair per file: two is ambiguous, and the
hook says so in its output rather than picking silently.
tooling_digest.//max_lines: Cap on injected digest lines. Defaults to 60. Over the cap the block is WITHHELD ENTIRELY and the overage is printed in its place — the session gets no map at all until the block is trimmed. That is deliberate: until 2026-09-14 the block was trimmed to the cap with a note appended, and the live map bled its tail because a trimmed block reads exactly like a complete one. Losing one session's map is loud; losing its tail is not. Trim the block rather than raising this number — it is paid for in every session. A second, fixed limit sits beside it: if everything the hook prints passes 9,500 characters (digest_lib.HARNESS_MAX_CHARS), the output is withheld the same way, because past ~10,000 the harness shows the model only a 2KB preview. No key moves that one.
tooling_digest.//stale_after_days: Days without an edit before the digest carries a 'treat these statuses as unverified' warning. Defaults to 90; 0 disables the check. An unreadable timestamp counts as fresh, so the hook never nags about a file it cannot actually assess. This exists because a stale registry is worse than no registry — it still gets trusted.

//enabled: Set false to stop noticing when MEMORY.md's hooks have drifted into a
second copy of the memories. Defaults to true; absent means on. Costs
nothing if you keep no memory directory — it only ever prints advice.
MEMORY.md is injected into every session while the memory files behind
it are read lazily, so the index is the only part with a standing token
price. The drift is specific and it recurs: a correction gets appended
to the HOOK instead of to the file the hook points at. Each append is
individually reasonable and invisible. Left alone, the
index keeps growing, and a single hook can end up longer than the
file it points at.
Silent on a healthy index, like memory-routing next door. It measures
two independent things: hook LENGTH (drift, scale-free) and the index's
TOTAL SIZE IN CHARACTERS (a hard ceiling in the harness). See both
thresholds below — they fire for different reasons and neither
substitutes for the other.
//max_hook_chars: A single hook longer than this is reported. Defaults to 200; absent
means 200. Deliberately well above the 120-160 routing target a hook
should sit at, because precision matters more than recall here: a
notice that fires on an ordinary session trains you to skip it.
Hook length is scale-free: it stays silent on a healthy corpus that
simply got bigger, and fires on a small one full of bloated hooks. It
names the thing you can fix.
CORRECTED 2026-09-14. This note used to end 'a flat byte cap would fire
on a healthy corpus that simply got bigger' and leave it there, which
read as an argument that no total-size cap should exist. The harness
imposes one regardless of what we think of it — see max_index_chars —
so a big tidy index is NOT healthy past that point, it is quietly
losing its last rows. The two thresholds are complementary, and this
file asserting otherwise is how the gap survived.
//max_index_chars: The whole index's budget, in CHARACTERS. Defaults to 24000; absent
means 24000; 0 or negative reads as unset, never as a cap everything
exceeds.
This one is not a style preference — it is a hard limit in the harness.
MEMORY.md is truncated at the TAIL, silently, with no error anywhere:
the last rows simply do not arrive in the session. The unit is
CHARACTERS, not bytes: the harness reports sizes as characters/1024
(KB), and it names its own limit '24.4KB', i.e. 25,000/1024 = 24.41,
so the constant is INFERRED to be 25,000 from that rounding while the
UNIT is observed.
24000 sits below the whole inferred band, so you are told while there
is still room to act rather than after a row has already gone missing.
Raising it toward 25,000 spends exactly that warning.
Measure with len(text), never `wc -c`: an index carries a multi-byte
em dash on EVERY row by format, so the byte count reads high —
enough to put a session on the wrong side of this threshold.
The fix when it fires depends on the layout memory-lint detects.
FLAT (no memory/topics/): retire a ROW, not shorten hooks — trimming
every hook to its target buys only a few rows, while deleting one that
duplicates a CLAUDE.md rule buys one outright. A file can keep existing without a row — put 'routed: false'
in its frontmatter and it stops being reported as an orphan.
TWO-LEVEL (memory/topics/ exists): move leaf rows out of MEMORY.md into
their topic files; MEMORY.md keeps only its Always rows and one row per
topic. 'routed: false' exempts nothing there — every file must be
reachable from Always or a nominated topic file.
ALSO read at edit time by context_growth's PostToolUse notice on
memory/MEMORY.md — one number for both tools, so they cannot disagree.
The harness also cuts at 200 LINES; that axis is max_index_lines below.
context_growth.overrides does not apply to MEMORY.md — it is a line map.
A value at or above 25000 is CLAMPED to 24999, for both tools: a cap
the index cannot cross before rows are already being dropped would
silence the only warning that the tail is being lost.
//distill_at_chars: The index size at which a session that starts fresh
(source startup or clear, never resume or compact) is told MEMORY.md is
near its cap and offered the memory-index-distill skill. Defaults to
19500; absent means 19500, and anything that is not a positive whole
Clamped: a value at or past max_index_chars is replaced by
max_index_chars minus 1000, so the notice can never arrive after the
cap it is meant to precede.
An absolute character count, deliberately not a fraction of
max_index_chars: the notice should land at a fixed distance from the
point where the harness starts dropping rows. Size = the larger of
chars and UTF-8 bytes (bytes in practice). 19500 lands it before
Claude Code's built-in "compact it now" notice, which starts at
//max_index_lines: The whole index's budget, in LINES as the harness counts them. Defaults
to 190; absent means 190; 0 or negative reads as unset.
The harness cuts MEMORY.md at 200 lines as well as ~25,000 chars,
whichever comes first, dropping the tail silently. READ from the 2.1.280
binary (2026-09-29): it trims the text, counts newlines + 1, and cuts
only past 200, so blank lines at either end do not count. memory-lint
counts the same way (lint_lib.harness_line_count), never splitlines().
With typical row lengths the character cap binds first; this catches an
190 leaves room to act before the cut. A value at or above 200 is
CLAMPED to 199, for the same reason as max_index_chars. Read by
memory-lint and by context_growth's edit-time notice — one key, both
//max_mean_hook_chars: Reported when the MEAN hook length exceeds this. Defaults to 170;
absent means 170. Catches the case no single hook triggers — uniform
creep across the whole index, which is what drift actually looks like
before any one hook becomes an outlier.
Structural faults (an orphaned memory file, a hook pointing at a file
that does not exist, a [[wikilink]] resolving to no memory, a row that
does not parse) are always reported regardless of these two numbers.
Those are defects rather than drift: an orphaned file is invisible to
every future session. Each category names at most 3 items and then
counts the rest, so one bad edit cannot turn the notice into a wall.
Setting either threshold to 0 does NOT disable it — 0 is treated as
unset and the default applies. Taken literally it would be the exact
opposite of what someone reaching for it wants: every hook exceeds 0,
so the whole index would be reported at every session start. Use
"enabled": false above to turn the notice off.

//max_lines: A staged CLAUDE.md over this many lines blocks the commit. Defaults to
800; absent means 800. THE one cap — since 2026-09-15 it applies to
every repo, because the shipped per-repo overrides below were deleted.
CLAUDE.md.template and policy/CLAUDE.md count too — they are what a new install gets.
800 is ~4x Anthropic's published guidance ('target under 200 lines per
CLAUDE.md file'; code.claude.com/docs/en/memory). That is a knowing
trade, not an oversight: per-repo caps set tight to current size made
every legitimate new rule a cut-or-raise negotiation. The structural fix
is path-scoped rules (.claude/rules/ with paths: frontmatter), which
load only when Claude touches matching files and cost nothing at
session start; until those land, 800 buys room without pretending the
attention cost is zero. The only limit Claude Code enforces is 4 MiB,
above which a CLAUDE.md is SKIPPED ENTIRELY.
Also checked by ci/local-checks.sh (the `context lint` check), not just
at commit time: the hook cannot catch a MERGE RACE (two PRs from one
base, each legitimately at cap, their sum over it).
This runs at COMMIT time, from the global pre-commit hook, not at
session start. That chain already carries several hooks, so
latency matters, and this check is irrelevant to the vast majority of sessions,
which never touch a CLAUDE.md. Growth happens in a commit; that is
where the signal belongs and where the trade can still be made.
It exists because adding a rule is free at write time and paid forever:
the file is injected into every session that loads it, and a file cut
hard grows straight back when the session adding to it has no signal
that a budget exists.
Fails OPEN, unlike the secret scanner sharing the same hook: a missed
size check costs a few dozen lines and is caught next commit, while a
line-counting tool wedging every commit on the machine costs
everything. git commit --no-verify is the documented override.
//overrides: Per-file caps for a repo that genuinely needs a different number than
max_lines above. Empty by default; an unmatched key gets max_lines.
Matched EXACTLY against two candidate keys in order:
1. <remote-owner>/<repo-name>/<path-within-repo>   (preferred)
2. <repo-name>/<path-within-repo>                  (fallback)
The repo name comes from git's --git-common-dir, so a linked worktree
keys the same as the primary checkout and the same commit cannot pass
or fail depending on where it was made. The owner comes from origin's
URL (SSH and HTTPS spellings both resolve to the same owner); a repo
with no origin has only the bare key.
WHY THE OWNER: a bare name cannot tell two CLONES apart. Two clones
of different repos that share a name would share one bare key, so a
cap meant for one lands on the other, and since this runs through a
global core.hooksPath it really is enforced there. Prefer the
qualified form; use the bare form only when you MEAN any clone by
that name. Where both are present the qualified one wins. The bare
form still matches, deliberately: dropping it would not error, it
would silently stop matching and hand the file the default.
TWO RULES. A lowered cap blocks the commit staging the file it
targets, including a PARTIAL cut, so it cannot land ahead of the cut
that earns it. RULE 1: a lowered cap moves in the SAME COMMIT as the
cut. RULE 2: it lands ABOVE the cut, never AT it. A cap equal to the
post-cut size is a wall on day one.
Exact, never a suffix: a suffix cannot tell a repo NAMED tools from
any repo that merely CONTAINS a directory of that name, and this
runs through a global core.hooksPath against every repo on the machine.
An unmatched key is not an error — it is a repo we have no opinion
about, and it gets the default above.
An override is a RATCHET, not an exemption. Size each just above
its file's current length so the check fires on GROWTH rather than
on a state nobody can fix in one commit; lower it as the file is
cut. A check that fires constantly is a check that gets ignored,
which is the same as no check at all.
An unversioned file (a workspace CLAUDE.md outside any repo) has no
repo component, so it cannot be keyed here. The context_growth
section below covers it, keyed by absolute path — a separate map,
deliberately, because the two key shapes cannot share one table.
//core_max_lines: A staged Core block over this many lines blocks the commit. Defaults to
A Core is the marker-delimited block at the top of a context file — the
part GUARANTEED to be read, and authoritative on its own: if Core and
body disagree, Core wins. So it is paid in full in every session that
loads the file, while the body is skimmed at best.
That is why its cap is SEPARATE from max_lines above and much tighter.
A 600-line file with an 80-line Core is fine; a 200-line file whose
Core is 150 lines is not, and one cap cannot express both.
//core_overrides: Per-file CORE caps, keyed and matched exactly as overrides above, and a
RATCHET for the same reason. Empty by default; an unmatched key gets
Deliberately empty rather than pre-populated: sizing a ratchet is a
judgment call against a file that has already been cut, and no real

advisory self-sufficiency check. Defaults to the four listed; absent
THIS LIST IS SEPARATE FROM THE FILES max_lines APPLIES TO, on purpose.
The whole-file cap covers CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.md.template only. This
list adds the tooling map, because TOOLING.md is the only file that
carries a Core today — leaving it out exempted the one file the Core
contract was written for from the one cap that enforces it.
Conflating the two lists is the mistake to avoid: a large TOOLING.md
runs to thousands of lines whole-file, so putting it under the
CLAUDE.md whole-file cap would report it far over on every single
edit. A notice that fires constantly is a notice nobody reads.
Matched on BASENAME, and checked BEFORE the file is read. In --staged

context_budget.//readings_path: Where `claude-context-budget --record` appends its one-line-per-day instruction reading, and where `--report` reads the log back from to compute a growth rate. Defaults to ~/.claude/context-budget/readings.jsonl. Absent means the default is used -- there is no way to opt out of the log entirely short of disabling the SessionStart hook itself, since a missing log just reads as 'no readings yet' rather than a fault.
//memory_dir: MEMORY.md. null (the default) means the resolver derives the slug from
workspace_root itself and refuses if that directory has no MEMORY.md.
(project or local level): the harness's precedence between those two
isn't reproduced here, so with the key present at that level the
resolver refuses to guess and the MEMORY.md row reports itself
unreadable until this is set explicitly. A USER-level value (in
writes) is resolved automatically instead -- this override is only
needed there if that value doesn't resolve to an existing directory.
//always_on_budget: The ceiling `--report`'s budget line compares the always-on
instruction total against (unit v2: sentences, plus 1 per Always
row). null (the default) prints "not set" and leaves the
edit-time notice off. Set, the context-growth hook notices when
an edit to an always-on surface raises the total past it, naming
There is deliberately no shipped default: Anthropic's only
documented anchor ("under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md") translates to
fewer sentences than policy/CLAUDE.md alone measures, so a
default set at the anchor could never pass. Set it from a measured
adherence sweep, not a picked number.
Only a positive JSON integer is accepted -- anything else (a bool,
a float, a string, zero or negative, a list) prints "invalid".

//enabled: Set false to stop the growth notice. Defaults to true; absent means on.
A PostToolUse hook, so it cannot block and does not try to — the point
is attribution, not refusal. It says nothing at all unless a count ROSE
past its cap in this session, or a new cross-reference appeared inside
a Core.
//memory_max_lines: The whole-file line cap for a memory/ entry (any file matching
memory/<name>.md, excluding MEMORY.md and memory/history/). Defaults to
280; absent means 280.
WHOLE-FILE ONLY. A memory entry gets NO Core cap — its Core half is
always None, never context_lint.core_max_lines' 80. A memory file
carries YAML frontmatter, not a CORE:START block, so a stray marker
pasted into one (from a pasted code fence, say) must not start billing
it against the CLAUDE.md family's Core budget, which is a different
contract for a different file. Do not add a memory core_max_lines key —
there is nothing for it to cap.
THE NOTICE FIRES AT THIS LIMIT, NEVER AT A FRACTION OF IT. There is no
percentage anywhere in this mechanism, and none belongs here. A file
that has just been distilled can still sit close under the cap, and a
fractional threshold (80% of 280 is 224) would fire on it: a notice
about a file that is already at a healthy size and not worth
distilling again. To choose your own cap, distill a few of your largest
memory files and see where they land; the cap belongs above that floor,
and the notice at the cap itself.
Per-file ratchets for individual memory files use the EXISTING
context_growth.overrides map above, keyed by absolute path — there is
no second map for memory. A memory file is outside git exactly like the
context files that map already serves, so it is consulted the same way
context_growth.core_overrides is NOT: a Core override keyed to a memory
file's path must not reintroduce a Core cap for one.
//rules_max_lines: The whole-file line cap for any .md under a .claude/rules/ directory,
versioned or not. Defaults to 200; absent means 200.
WHOLE-FILE ONLY, no Core cap — same shape as memory_max_lines above,
and for the same reason: a rules file carries no CORE:START block, so
a stray marker inside one must not start billing it against the
200 is this toolkit's own default for a rules file, borrowed from
Anthropic's under-200-lines guidance for a CLAUDE.md file -- Anthropic
sets no per-rules-file limit. Chosen over 800 (the CLAUDE.md default)
and 120 (too aggressive for a file that may cover a real topic).
The missing-paths: notice below fires regardless of this value — it is
not a size check, and applies even to a rules file well under this cap.
Per-file ratchets use the EXISTING context_growth.overrides map above,
keyed by absolute path — there is no second map for rules files either.
//overrides: Per-file WHOLE-FILE caps for context files that are in NO git repo,
keyed by ABSOLUTE PATH. Empty by default; an unmatched file falls back
to context_lint.max_lines.
A SEPARATE MAP from context_lint.overrides, and they must not be
merged: that one is keyed <repo-name>/<path-within-repo>, this one by
absolute path, and the two key shapes cannot coexist in one table.
context_lint's cap resolver returns the default BEFORE consulting
overrides whenever the key is null — which it is, by construction, for
every file outside a repo — so without this map no per-file cap was
expressible for the very files this hook exists to reach.
Consulted ONLY for files outside a repo. A versioned file already has a
working ratchet in context_lint.overrides and does not get a second
one, or the two maps silently compete over the same file.
Keys are ~-expanded and realpath'd on BOTH sides before comparing.
Both sides because on macOS /var is a symlink to /private/var, so
resolving one side makes the key match nothing, silently. ~-expanded
because config reads of a MAP do not expand paths — only scalar path
reads do — so a key written the way a human writes it arrives verbatim.
A RATCHET, not an exemption, exactly as in context_lint.overrides. Size
each entry just above its file's current length so the check fires on
GROWTH rather than on a state nobody can fix in one edit, and lower it
as the file is cut.
//core_overrides: The same, for CORE caps on files outside any repo. Empty by default.
An unmatched file falls back to context_lint.core_max_lines — except
the tooling map, whose Core cap is tooling_digest.max_lines.
TWO CORE CAPS, DELIBERATELY. A CLAUDE.md's Core is capped by
tooling_digest.max_lines, which already exists and is the number past
which the digest hook WITHHOLDS the injected block entirely (it
trimmed to it until 2026-09-14). Do not unify
them: a second number for the same file is a second number to drift.
The map's TEMPLATE resolves through the same digest budget, not
core_max_lines: a template is capped by what it germinates into, since
/onboard copies its Core into a real map.
//state_path: Where the hook records last-seen counts per file. null (the default)
resolves to ~/.claude/context-growth-state.json.
WHY IT EXISTS AT ALL: the hook fires on GROWTH, and growth is not
visible in a single post-edit snapshot. PostToolUse receives the tool
input, not the pre-edit content, so the prior size has to be recorded
somewhere. Without it the check degrades to a STATE check — over cap or
not — which fires on every edit to a file that is already over,
including the edits that shrink it. A notice that fires constantly is a
notice nobody reads, which is the failure this whole contract exists to
remove.
One entry per absolute path, holding its last-seen line count, Core
count and dangling-reference list. Growth is bounded by dropping
entries whose file no longer exists on each write; that is the whole
pruning policy. Writes are atomic (temp file in the target's own
directory, then a rename) and there is deliberately NO LOCK: two
sessions may edit at once, a lost update costs one missed advisory
notice, and a lock in a best-effort hook can wedge an editor for a
message nobody is blocked on.
CLAUDE_CONTEXT_GROWTH_STATE overrides this, ahead of config. It exists
for the test suite: a suite that mutates the real state file is the
ambient-state defect in another costume.

//enabled: Set false to stop nudging when a write to a memory/ entry looks like it
records a config fact that belongs in TOOLING.md instead. Defaults to
true; absent means on. Costs nothing if you don't keep a TOOLING.md —
it only ever prints advice, never blocks a write.
It is a NUDGE, not a gate, and deliberately so. Preventing the write
would need a PreToolUse deny driven by a keyword heuristic, and a guard
that rejects legitimate memory writes gets switched off — at which point
it protects nothing.
Tuned for PRECISION over recall. A reminder that fires on ordinary memory writes
trains you to skip it, which is worse than silence. If you widen the
signal list in routing_lib.py, re-measure against your own memory corpus
before shipping, since a broad list mostly fires on noise.
Hold a macOS sleep assertion while a Claude Code turn is actually
running, so a long build survives being walked away from. Defaults to
FALSE, and absent means off — unlike every other feature here.
Inheriting a machine that stops sleeping is a surprise nobody asked
for, and the cost of it being off is one interrupted build rather than
a laptop that runs hot in a bag.
The screensaver is NOT what breaks a long run — processes run fine
behind it. SYSTEM SLEEP is, and the stock settings make them look
linked: the display sleeps on its idle timer and the system follows a
minute later. `pmset -g custom` shows both numbers for your machine.
Each session holds the Mac awake for 30 minutes after its last
activity (hold_seconds), and each background job Claude started holds
it until that job finishes, capped at 1 hour (job_hold_seconds). Holds
are bound with `caffeinate -w`, so the kernel ends one the moment its
session or job exits and a crashed session cannot leak one. Power
assertions are additive: the machine sleeps once the LAST hold ends.
It never prevents DISPLAY sleep — the screen still goes dark, only the
machine stays up. And closing the lid sleeps it regardless.
//require_ac: Only hold the assertion while plugged in. Defaults to true. Set false
to keep a build alive on battery too, which drops `-s` and holds only
`-i` — the man page says `-s` is valid on AC power alone, so asking
for it on battery is asking for nothing.
`/caffeinate on` and `/caffeinate off` write this key, which is the
whole reason that command exists. `on` also sets `enabled` to true,
because setting only this one on a machine that never opted in would
Unplugging mid-session RELEASES the running hold at the next hook,
rather than merely declining to renew it. Otherwise the answer would
depend on whether you unplugged before or after the turn started.
Note that closing the lid sleeps the Mac no matter what this says.
Clamshell sleep ignores both flags; only `pmset disablesleep` blocks
it, which this deliberately does not touch.
//battery_override_hours: How long `/caffeinate on` lasts before lapsing back to wall-power-only.
Defaults to 24. Set 0 to make it permanent until `/caffeinate off`.
Negative and non-numeric fall back to 24.
THE CLOCK RESTARTS ON USE, not on the command: any hold actually taken
on battery pushes it out again. So working unplugged every day keeps it
alive indefinitely, and a day without unplugging retires it. That rule
rests on forgetting the setting and not using it being the same
event — a fixed 24 hours from the
command would retire it mid-trip for anyone who actually works on
battery. Working on WALL POWER never refreshes it, because that is not
using the override.
A lapse RELEASES holds already running, it does not merely decline to
take new ones. Otherwise a session open at the moment of expiry would
keep the machine awake indefinitely, which is the whole failure this
exists to stop.
The clock lives in the state directory (battery-override.json), NOT in
this file, because the refresh-on-use rule means a HOOK maintains it and
a hook that edits this file — from every concurrent session, to record a
routine event — is a risk not worth taking for a convenience. Deleting
that file costs one fresh 24-hour window, never your configuration.
This does NOT touch `enabled`. Wall-power holding is unaffected by the
lapse; only the battery override retires.
//battery_floor_percent: Release the hold when the battery falls to this, and decline to take a
new one until it charges past. Defaults to 20. Set 0 to disable the
floor entirely. Consulted only on battery — on wall power there is
nothing to run flat, so a low charge there is simply a laptop charging.
ZERO IS MEANINGFUL here, unlike the *_seconds keys where it falls back:
'no floor' is a thing you can want, a zero deadline is not. Values
outside 0-100 fall back to 20 rather than clamping, because a floor of
150 is a typo and honouring it would release every hold instantly —
indistinguishable from the feature being broken.
This exists because `require_ac: false` is machine-wide and persistent.
Every window left open then holds on battery until its session exits,
and a laptop left open overnight is the case that costs something. The
trade is real and worth knowing: a long unattended build on battery
DIES here rather than running the machine flat.
//settle_seconds: How long an UNBOUND hold lasts after a turn ends. Defaults to 300
(5 minutes). Non-numeric, zero and negative all fall back to that.
Read that first word carefully, because this key is narrower than it
looks. A hold bound to a live `claude` process is NOT shortened when a
turn ends — it runs out its idle timer (hold_seconds), and background
jobs carry their own holds (job_hold_seconds). This window applies only
when the walk up to the `claude` process failed and the hold has no
`-w` to release it, so its deadline is the only bound it has.
That makes this a fallback rather than the main path. If you want an
idle session sleeping sooner, lower hold_seconds instead — that is the
idle timer a normal, bound hold actually ends on.
//hold_seconds: The idle timer: how long a session's hold lasts after its LAST
activity. Defaults to 1800 (30 minutes). Zero, negative and non-numeric
all fall back to 1800: a zero deadline would expire before it is
recorded, so the timer can be raised but never removed.
Activity is a prompt or a tool batch, and batches inside dispatched
subagents count. It is re-armed at most every 2 minutes (or half this
value, if smaller), so the machine sleeps up to that much EARLY: 28-30
minutes after the last activity at the default. With several sessions
open, it runs from the last activity in any of them.
Background jobs Claude launched get their own hold (job_hold_seconds),
so this timer is only the fallback for work that is running but was
not detected. Raise it if you run long work it cannot see. Do not set
it absurdly high in place of removing it: a hold with neither a live
process nor a deadline is the mistake nobody notices.
//job_hold_seconds: Cap on the hold for ONE background job. Defaults to 3600 (1 hour).
A background job is a command Claude started with run_in_background (a
Codex gate, a test run, a build). Each gets its own hold, bound to the
job's process, so it ends the moment the job does. This cap ends it
anyway if the job hangs or never exits (a dev server, a stuck call). A
job is never re-held after its cap: one that runs longer is covered
only by the idle timer above.
//state_dir: One small json file per session recording which assertion belongs to
it, and which `claude` process that assertion was bound to. Defaults to
Deleting the directory is nearly harmless. A BOUND assertion carries
`-w` and dies with its session whether or not anything on disk points
at it — measured 2026-08-27, it releases in ~0s even when the session is
SIGKILLed, because the kernel does that and no hook is involved.
An UNBOUND one is the exception, and it is the only hold on the machine
with no kernel backstop: the walk to the `claude` process can fail, and
that hold has only its `hold_seconds` deadline. Delete its record and
nothing sweeps the `caffeinate` process it named, so at worst the machine
stays awake until that deadline expires. Nothing is corrupted either way:
the next prompt in each session writes a fresh record and rebinds.

build_cost.//enabled: Set false to stop the SessionEnd hook recording anything. Absent means enabled. This is the only supported off switch: install.sh merges the whole SessionEnd event as a unit, so removing the hook from ~/.claude/settings.json by hand is undone on the next install.
build_cost.//ledger_path: Where one line per session is appended, split four ways (main, executor, review, other). A session, not a build: a long session can span several builds, and a resumed session appends a superseding row rather than a duplicate. Written by the `claude-build-cost-record` SessionEnd hook, and by `claude-build-cost` itself unless you pass --no-record. Defaults to ~/.claude/build-costs.jsonl. The file is only ever appended to, never rewritten, so it is safe to point at something you keep.
build_cost.//qualifying_agent_types: Which subagent agentTypes make a session worth recording at SessionEnd. A session with none of these wrote no build worth measuring, so no ledger row is appended. Defaults to executor, task-reviewer, workflow-subagent, code-reviewer, architect-reviewer and spec-reviewer when the key is absent or is not a list of strings; an empty list falls back to the same default rather than recording nothing. A name matches with or without the `toolkit-build:` plugin prefix. The two review-lane types are in the default because without them a session that ran a /build review gate and wrote no code records nothing at all, so the ledger under-samples exactly the review-heavy sessions a cost argument needs. architect-reviewer is in it for the same reason: a session that ran only that optional reviewer would otherwise record nothing. spec-reviewer (2026-11-21) is the design/plan gates' Agent fallback reviewer; a config that lists this key explicitly does not pick up a type added to the default later, so add it by hand. Each row carries TWO fields, answering different questions. `agent_types` is every agentType observed — a fact about the session, config-independent — and is what `--ledger` derives its `build`/`gate` kind column from; classifying off the config-dependent field instead meant anyone who dropped `executor` from this list got every build of theirs labelled `gate` with no symptom. `qualified_by` is the intersection with THIS list, i.e. why the row exists at all — an audit trail for the recording gate, never a classification input. Note `workflow-subagent` is any workflow agent, not a /build lens specifically, so `gate` means the session wrote no code, NOT that it ran a /build gate.

session_claim.//enabled: Set false to stop claiming checkouts entirely. Defaults to true; absent means on. On is the stricter setting here — the risk it prevents is a PR containing another session's work, and the cost of a misfire is one momentary block that the circuit breaker below bounds.
session_claim.//max_blocks: Blocks per session before the guard stands down for the rest of that session. A CORRECT block happens once — you relocate to a worktree and nothing contends again — so repeated blocks mean relocation is not working. Defaults to 3. Setting 0 disables the breaker, which also removes the only bound on what a bug in this tool can cost you.

session_titler.//enabled: Set false to stop titling sessions at SessionEnd entirely — no worker forked, no model call, no custom-title record, no index row. Defaults to true; absent means on. When on, each ended session with at least two real user messages costs one `claude -p --model haiku` call, run detached so it never delays the session's exit. The title is a short outcome phrase with no prefix; an answer that reads as prose is discarded, leaving the session untitled.
session_titler.//index_path: Where `csearch` keeps its searchable index of past session titles.

usage_watch.//enabled: Set false to turn the whole feature off — no status-line cache write, no tier warnings, no subagent headroom, no postmortem handover. Defaults to true; absent means on.
usage_watch.//thresholds: Utilisation percentages at which the notice/gate/halt tiers start (inclusive). Defaults are 70/85/95. If you set them out of order, they are SORTED rather than obeyed — a halt below a gate would make the halt tier unreachable, and the strictest configured number should still bite.
usage_watch.//cache_path: Where claude-usage-line writes the budget snapshot it renders. Defaults to ~/.claude/usage-budget.json. This is the ONLY file that writes here; do not point it at the same path as state_path below.
usage_watch.//state_path: Where the hooks record what tier they have already announced, so a session isn't nagged on every tool batch. Defaults to ~/.claude/usage-budget-state.json. Kept separate from cache_path on purpose — the status line rewrites its file every 30s, which would race a hook's write to a shared file.
usage_watch.//stale_after_seconds: How old the cached snapshot may be before a hook treats it as absent. Defaults to 900 (15 minutes). An expired rate-limit WINDOW is already discarded by resets_at; this catches the other case — a cache whose window hasn't reset yet but whose reading predates a laptop sleep or a long gap with no status-line refresh, so it can no longer be trusted as current. Being treated as absent is no longer the same as being ignored: see unknown_reannounce_seconds.
usage_watch.//unknown_reannounce_seconds: How long a session goes before it is told AGAIN that the budget cannot be read at all. Defaults to 43200 (12 hours), which is once per working session in practice; a value of 0 or less falls back to that default rather than meaning 'every turn'. An hourly cadence assumes unknown is a transient state worth re-checking; on any surface without a status line it is PERMANENT, so hourly is a permanent nag, and a warning that repeats without being actionable is what teaches a reader to skim it. Keep any replacement value FINITE: the expiry shares the resets_at slot a real window uses so the state file's pruning collects it, and a never-expiring bucket is the one entry that would grow that file without bound. An unreadable budget is the normal state on any surface without a status line — the VS Code extension and the desktop app both render none — and the hooks now say so instead of going quiet, because silence is indistinguishable from having headroom. Unknown is a standing condition rather than an event, so unlike a tier crossing it is deduped on BOTH UserPromptSubmit and PostToolBatch; repeating it every turn is how a warning teaches its reader to skim past it. TWO CASES WHERE THE NOTICE WILL NEVER CLEAR, and you want 'enabled': false instead of a longer window: you kept a custom statusLine that does not pipe through claude-usage-line, and API-key authentication, where rate-limit data never reaches any surface at all. A momentary five-hour ROLLOVER is not one of these — an incomplete reading in an otherwise healthy session is handled separately and never spends this window.
usage_watch.//subagent_context: Set false to stop telling each dispatched subagent its budget headroom on SubagentStart. Defaults to true; absent means on.
usage_watch.//postmortem_handover: Set false to stop writing a handover document when a turn dies with reason rate_limit or billing_error. Defaults to true; absent means on.
usage_watch.//transcript_root: Where Claude Code writes transcript JSONL, which the budget estimator reads to count output tokens. Defaults to ~/.claude/projects; exists mainly so tests never touch the real corpus.
usage_watch.//estimate: Set true to enable the transcript-based budget estimate. DEFAULTS TO FALSE; absent means OFF. Anchor it: run `claude-usage-anchor <pct> --resets-in <duration>` (e.g. `45 --resets-in 4h20m`) with the 5-hour figure and reset time from the Account & Usage panel, or let a terminal status line record one. It adds this machine's output tokens since that reading (de-duplicated by message.id, subagents included) as a drift: ONE figure, labelled an estimate and a floor, since other machines and the web app spend the same budget unseen. No idle-gap or phase inference: with no live anchor it reports nothing. A percentage needs a ratio, measured from two readings in one window 5+ points apart, or default_ratio below; else tokens only. Wherever there is no real reading, on any surface, it fires the notice/gate/halt tiers with the same obligations as a real reading.
usage_watch.//dispatch_advisory: Set true to forecast a dispatch against the usage budget: a PreToolUse hook on Agent|Workflow that reports headroom, what this lane has historically cost, and whether it fits. DEFAULTS TO FALSE; absent means OFF, because this is the only hook that can return permissionDecision "ask" and interrupt a human. PreToolUse fires before the tool RUNS, not before the model DECIDES, so below halt the forecast informs your NEXT dispatch; only the "ask" at halt stops the call it fires on. It asks at halt on a real reading or an anchored estimate (see `estimate`, a separate switch); with neither it says nothing. If the hook crashes it prints a crash report saying the dispatch was NOT checked. Cost history comes from `build_cost.ledger_path` (5 sessions per lane before a figure shows). A real reading gates on whichever of the 5-hour and 7-day windows binds; an estimate covers the 5-hour window only.
usage_watch.//anchor_path: Where anchor readings are recorded for the estimator: the latest reading, the first reading of the same window, and the measured ratio. Written by `claude-usage-anchor <pct> --resets-in <duration>` and by a terminal status line. Deliberately a different file from state_path: two hooks doing read-modify-write on one file would drop each other's writes. Defaults to ~/.claude/usage-anchors.json.
usage_watch.//default_ratio: Optional, and null on purpose: output tokens per 1% of the 5-hour window, used only until this machine has measured its own from two readings in one window at least 5 points apart. NO DEFAULT SHIPS, because the figure depends on your plan and account and nobody publishes it. Set it only if you have worked yours out (output tokens counted the way estimate_lib.scan_usage counts them, divided by the percentage points they moved the Account & Usage panel). A measured ratio still wins over it, and an estimate that uses it says so. Set it with `--set usage_watch.default_ratio=<whole number>`; the setter takes integers only. Null, absent, boolean, non-numeric, zero or negative all mean no ratio. If the counting ever changes, a ratio fitted to the old counting is wrong too: re-derive it, never rescale it.
usage_watch.//codex_low_gates: Announces once per session, on UserPromptSubmit, when the estimated Codex review-gate budget falls to this many gates left or below. An estimate needs a fitted per-gate cost for your plan, window and model, and this toolkit ships none (see tools/codex-review/codex_review_lib.py, CALIBRATIONS), so until you fit one the Codex notice instead fires once the window passes 90% used and again at 100%. Defaults to 15; absent means 15. 0 means only the 100% notice. Silent when there is no Codex rollout log to read (no ~/.codex/sessions, or CODEX_HOME set to an empty tree). Bool, non-integer or negative values fall back to 15 rather than erroring.

base_pin.//enabled: Set false to silence the mid-session notice that origin/<default> is ahead of the worktree you are working in, and to stop its background fetch. Defaults to true; absent means on. This is the companion to repo_freshness, not a duplicate: that hook's repo-behind notice fires at session start and only when you are ON the default branch (bar a toolkit checkout pinned by ./install.sh --rollback, which it always names), so it is silent for the entire life of a feature branch. This one fires only in a LINKED WORKTREE, which is exactly where that gap matters — every worktree of a repo shares one set of origin/* refs, so another session merging moves your base without touching your files.
base_pin.//fetch_interval_seconds: How stale the last `git fetch` may be before a new one is spawned in the background. Defaults to 14400 (4 hours). The fetch NEVER blocks the prompt — the count is taken from refs already on disk — so a longer interval only means finding out one prompt later. The clock is PER-WORKTREE, not per-repo: FETCH_HEAD is a per-worktree pseudo-ref, so the age is read from the same place this tool's own fetch writes it. That is the invariant that matters — an earlier version read the repo's common dir while fetching into the worktree, so the clock never advanced and it spawned a fetch on EVERY prompt submit, forever, with no output. The cost of getting it right is that N worktrees each fetch once per interval instead of one between them, which is a few cheap calls; a shared clock would mean deriving a primary-checkout path by stripping a component off --git-dir, and that guesses wrong under --separate-git-dir.
base_pin.//max_commits_listed: How many of the new commits to name in the notice, newest first. Defaults to 5. Set 0 to report only the count. The subject lines are what make the notice actionable rather than merely true — "3 commits ahead" is a number, "#78, #79, #80" is a reason to merge.
base_pin.//state_path: Where the dedupe table lives. Defaults to ~/.claude/base-pin-state.json. Keyed by session and checkout, holding the last origin/<default> sha announced there, so the notice speaks once per move and re-speaks the next time the default branch moves. Records older than 7 days are pruned on read. Deliberately a different file from usage_watch state_path: two hooks doing read-modify-write on one file would drop each other's writes. Deleting it is harmless — it costs one repeated notice per live session.

model_guard.//enabled: Set false to stop claude-model-guard refusing an Agent dispatch that names no model. Defaults to true; ABSENT MEANS ON, and a config file that will not parse also leaves it on — a broken config must not be a way to disarm a guard. What it refuses: an `Agent` call with no `model` runs on the session's model, so on an Opus session it pays Opus rates for work that is usually Sonnet's, and nothing in the transcript says so. It is DEFINITION-AWARE, so an agent whose own frontmatter pins a concrete model dispatches cleanly with no argument at the call site; only a dispatch that would genuinely fall back to the session model is refused. Note that `model: inherit` in a definition is NOT a pin — it means 'use the session model', which is the case being guarded against, and it is common in plugin agent definitions. `Workflow` is deliberately never judged: its per-agent models live inside a JavaScript string, and denying one would be a denial on a guess. To bypass it, re-run the session with MODEL_GUARD_ALLOW=1 set — that is a launch-time, session-wide switch, not a per-call override, because a PreToolUse hook can only read the environment it inherited from the Claude Code process.

load_guard.//enabled: Gates whether install.sh creates the shims: a symlink ~/.local/bin/<tool> -> claude-heavy-run for each heavy tool (built-in: ffmpeg, whisper-cli, llama-server, llama-cli, llama-bench; plus `commands` below), so a bare call runs under a one-at-a-time lock and a memory floor. A shim is made only if the real tool is on PATH outside ~/.local/bin, and an existing ~/.local/bin/<tool> that is not already our shim is never replaced (the installer warns). Defaults to true; ABSENT MEANS ON, and a config file that will not parse leaves it on. Set false and the next install.sh run removes the shims. Limit: a call by absolute path (/opt/homebrew/bin/ffmpeg) bypasses the shim. `claude-heavy-run CMD ...` always takes its lock, with or without a shim.
load_guard.//min_available_gb: A job is refused when available memory (kern.memorystatus_level percent x hw.memsize, read with sysctl) is below `--needs-gb N` plus this floor. Absent or non-numeric = 3. 3 GB is an UNMEASURED starting value: on a 16 GB Mac the idle working load (VS Code, Chrome, Claude) measured about 6 GB available on 2026-11-27, so tune this against real jobs. An unreadable memory figure makes the job refuse (exit 75), never run: the floor is a safety value.
load_guard.//commands: Extra tool names that get a shim, added to the built-in set. Matched by basename (a path is reduced to its name), and the shim exists only while a real tool of that name is on PATH. Takes effect on the next install.sh run. Absent = built-in set only.
load_guard.//state_dir: Where heavy-run.lock lives; it also holds the running job's pid, command and start time. Must be an ABSOLUTE path once ~ and $VARS are expanded: a relative path or an unset variable makes every job refuse (exit 75), never fall back. Absent = ~/.claude/load-guard, created if missing. The lock is an flock held by the job itself, so a crash leaves no stale lock. Deleting the lock file does NOT stop the running job and lets a second one start; wait for the pid the refusal names.

wrap_up.//repos_root: Where your git checkouts live. claude-wrap-up-survey surveys the immediate subdirectories containing a working tree (never recursed into; bare repos are skipped because they cannot hold unsaved work), and claude-backup leaves this folder out of the workspace copy, since each checkout's remote holds it. ~ and $VARS are expanded. null, absent or "" means <workspace_root>/repos. A value that is not an absolute path after expansion (relative, or naming an unset variable) is refused, never replaced by the default. No workspace_root and no value, a refused value, or a path that does not exist all produce `surveyed: false` with a reason -- never an empty result. That distinction is the whole point: /wrap-up reports whether it is safe to shut down, so 'looked and found nothing' and 'never looked' must never render the same way. A typo here would otherwise certify a machine as clean while examining nothing.
wrap_up.//note: This tool takes no thresholds and writes nothing. It is read-only by construction -- it shells out only to `git` with read-only verbs, never fetches, and never calls `gh`. Resolving whether a branch ahead of the default branch is actually unmerged is left to the caller precisely because that needs the network, and a squash merge makes git alone answer wrongly.

toolkit_integrity.//enabled: Set false to silence claude-toolkit-integrity entirely — BOTH halves, including the one that tells you a guard has gone dark, plus the guard-coverage and SessionStart canary checks. Defaults to true; absent means on. Think twice: Claude Code silently SKIPS a hook it cannot execute, so a dangling ~/.local/bin/claude-danger-guard is indistinguishable from a guard that simply had nothing to say. If the drift notice is what bothers you, turn off drift_notice below instead and keep this one.
toolkit_integrity.//drift_notice: Set false to keep the integrity check and drop only the notice that the toolkit's HEAD moved mid-session. Defaults to true; absent means on. Split from `enabled` on purpose, because the two halves are not worth the same: the integrity half catches a dark guard, this half is a convenience telling you the tooling around your work changed while your own branch and edits did not. The notice is already path-filtered to tools/, agents/, skills/, lib/, every plugin's hooks/hooks.json (plugin/ and plugin-*/) and claude/profiles.json, so a docs-only or tests-only merge says nothing — an unfiltered version on a checkout that moves often fires constantly and teaches you to skim past it.
toolkit_integrity.//state_path: Where the dedupe table lives. Defaults to ~/.claude/toolkit-integrity-state.json. Keyed by session, holding the last set of problems announced, the last toolkit HEAD seen, and the last canary result, so each half speaks when its subject CHANGES and never repeats on an unchanged one — a second link breaking mid-session is a new notice, not a suppressed duplicate. Records older than 7 days are pruned on read. Deliberately a different file from base_pin state_path even though the shape is identical: one on-disk format shared between two tools means a schema change in either can break the other after only one was read. Deleting it is harmless — it costs one repeated notice per live session.

//enabled: Set true to remind Claude, right before it dispatches a subagent, to
sharpen that subagent's instructions with the prompt-optimizer skill.
A subagent starts with none of the conversation's context, so a vague
dispatch prompt fails silently instead of asking a follow-up question.
Defaults to false; absent means off, and only a literal JSON true turns
it on. It is a nudge, not a guard, so the default is silence.
The reminder needs the prompt-optimizer skill installed. Enabled with no
skill, the hook prints nothing, and ./install.sh and ./install.sh --check
say the reminder is enabled but inert. It reminds; it never runs the
skill or claims that optimization happened.

//models: Which Codex model each full-power review gate runs on. null keeps the
toolkit's default (code: gpt-5.6-terra; merge, plan, design, architecture:
gpt-6-astra). Set one when your Codex account does not serve a
default: claude-codex-review exits 4 and names the gate. A value is a
model name: a non-empty string with no whitespace, not starting with
'-'. Anything else, or a key that is not one of those five gates, makes
claude-codex-review refuse (exit 2) before it dispatches. The four
/build gates read it only under build.review = "full-power";
architecture reads it whenever an architecture review runs on Codex.

//enabled: Set true to let claude-harness-check's PostToolBatch/UserPromptSubmit
hook (--hook) advise when the running Claude Code binary has not yet
been re-verified against the memory behaviour this toolkit relies on
(MEMORY.md cut at 200 lines and at 25,000 characters, each probed on
its own, topic files not injected,
path-scoped rules loading only on a matching read, archive files never
loading, and auto memory loading from the configured directory).
Defaults to false; absent means off, and the hook exits 0
before reading any of its own state while this is unset or not literal
true — a config typo can never turn it on by accident.
The notice, when on, names claude-harness-check: run it by hand (no
flag) to re-verify the current version. That costs three Haiku runs
against a throwaway fixture project, about a minute, and records a
pass/partial/fail per version; pass and partial both stop the notice,
and partial means user-level memory resolution was not verified.
Off by default because it is a maintainer's check: run
claude-harness-check after a Claude Code upgrade if you change the
toolkit itself; otherwise leave this false and never see the notice.

//destination: Where claude-backup copies your machine-local files: the workspace root
(minus wrap_up.repos_root), every Claude Code auto-memory directory, this
config file and Claude Code's settings.json. NO DEFAULT, on purpose: null
or absent means the tool refuses (exit 2) rather than guess a folder.
The folder must already exist; the tool never creates it. A folder your
takes the copy off this machine; the tool does not check that it does.
Binary files are never copied (they cannot be scanned for secrets), so
keep those somewhere else that is backed up.
backup.//keep: How many backups to retain per machine. Defaults to 8; absent, non-numeric or below 1 means 8.
backup.//max_age_days: --status reports a backup older than this as stale (exit 1), and /wrap-up then takes a new one. Defaults to 7; absent, non-numeric or below 1 means 7.
backup.//extra_paths: Further paths to back up on top of the built-in set. Defaults to []; absent means nothing extra.
backup.//exclude: Glob patterns to skip on top of the built-in excludes (.venv*, node_modules, .git, .env, *.pem, *.key and similar), matched against each file or folder name and against its path inside the backed-up item. Defaults to []; absent means built-in excludes only.

//fixture_root: Where `claude-index-distill prove` builds its throwaway fixture: a copy of
your memory directory and rule pages, with the manifest applied. Defaults to
<system temp>/claude-index-distill/; absent (or null) means that default.
Every proof removes its own fixture on exit unless `--keep` is passed, so
the copies of real memory do not linger. The grader's empty cwd is made here
too. Each `prove` starts by deleting any dir here named exactly like one it
makes (index-distill-<8 chars>, index-distill-grader-<8 chars>): what a
killed run left behind, and any fixture an earlier `--keep` kept. It prints
each path it removes. It sweeps only while holding a lock on `.prove.lock`
here (the file stays), so a second `prove` refuses while one is running.
